content: Hair-grooming syncope, also referred to as hair-combing syncope, is a specific type of fainting disorder that occurs during activities such as combing or brushing the hair. This condition is most commonly observed in children between the ages of five and sixteen. It typically begins with presyncopal symptoms, such as lightheadedness or dizziness, during hair-related activities like combing, brushing, braiding, trimming, curling, or blow-drying. These symptoms may then progress to a loss of consciousness and, in some cases, convulsions. Additional symptoms that may precede or follow these episodes include migraines, abdominal pain, a sensation of feeling funny, or blurred vision. The underlying mechanisms potentially responsible for this condition include pain or nerve stimulation on the scalp, which is thought to be similar to the mechanism of parade-ground syncope. Another possible cause is the compression of blood vessels or nerves due to neck flexion or extension during hair grooming. A study conducted in 2009 identified 111 pediatric cases of hair-grooming syncope in the United States. Approximately 75% of these cases occurred in female patients. The study also noted that in males, the condition was most commonly associated with hair cutting, whereas in females, it was more frequently linked to hair brushing. Hair-grooming syncope is sometimes misdiagnosed as epilepsy; however, it is more accurately classified as a paroxysmal non-epileptic event. It may also have a connection to orthostatic hypotension, but it is not associated with any abnormalities of the heart. This condition has been proposed as a potential explanation for the so-called hair-brushing syndrome, an extremely rare phenomenon in which static electricity is alleged to disrupt brain or organ function. To date, only two cases of hair-brushing syndrome have been reported globally. One of these cases gained media attention in 2011 when the Daily Mail published a sensationalized claim that hair brushing could potentially lead to death.
